A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, model framework, and retained experiments. All 17 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, gridness measurements, assumption ablations, topological analyses, and path-integration results, including Appendix A.7.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds analyses of learned representations and recorded rodent grid-cell activity in Sections 3.4–3.5 and Appendix A.10.

M1.justification: v1 offers an alternative cosine-based conformal-isometry loss in Equation 6; v2 drops this option while retaining the distance-based loss, recurrent models, and conformal modulation. This narrows the proposed loss formulations without establishing that the retained experiments used a changed procedure.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates simulated spatial representations and path integration. v2 additionally analyzes real rodent neural recordings from Gardner et al. (2021), using a 93-cell module in Section 3.5 and another module in Appendix A.10. This substantially extends empirical coverage to biological population activity.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same comparison methods: Banino et al. (2018), Sorscher et al. (2023), and Gao et al. (2021). The added analyses introduce no additional competing methods, and the existing ablation and re-encoding comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New diagnostic protocols compare neural and physical displacement using linear and quadratic fits. Section 3.4 samples displacements in (0, 0.125) for the linear model with s = 10; Section 3.5 also examines recorded activity norms. Existing training settings and the 100-step, 300-trajectory path-integration evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 3.4–3.5 add direct tests of whether learned and recorded representations satisfy local conformal isometry, including deviations at larger displacements and approximate constancy of population activity norms. Appendix A.10 checks another recorded module. These substantially extend assumption validation beyond the retained Figure 3 ablations and topological analysis.

E5.justification: The path-integration uncertainty display is retained, with no added seed counts, repeated-training information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new neural-norm standard deviation describes variation in the measured activity itself; it does not introduce uncertainty estimates for model performance or fitted relationships.

E6.justification: v2 adds findings of approximately linear local displacement relationships in learned and recorded representations, finite-displacement deviations, and recorded activity norms with mean 128.6 and standard deviation 15.1, or 0.12 after mean normalization. These are substantial new biological and geometric results. Tables 1–2 and the appendix path-integration errors remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the exact local-distance formulation with an asymptotic definition and replaces much of v1's square-versus-hexagon Fourier argument with fourth-order flat-torus analysis. Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendices A.5–A.6 add derivative proofs, a symmetry theorem, and a fixed-average-curvature optimality argument. The earlier restriction from equal-length primitive vectors to only square or hexagonal lattices is removed.

C1.justification: v1 presents theory as supporting the conformal-isometry hypothesis and identifies the minimal-setting investigation as its main contribution. v2's abstract, introduction, and contribution discussion assert that hexagonal patterns emerge through loss minimization because the hexagonal flat torus minimizes deviation from local isometry. This substantially strengthens and refocuses the central theoretical claim.

C2.justification: v2 shifts the mechanism explanation toward extrinsic curvature, directional isotropy, and loss minimization, replacing v1's Fourier-based preference and frequency-packing discussion. It interprets recorded activity as approximate support for the assumptions while acknowledging noise and incomplete cell sampling. The existing limitations concerning other neural systems and variable spatial metrics are largely retained in Appendix A.2.

D1.justification: Appendix A.9.1 explicitly documents block-diagonal B(theta), with each block corresponding to a module. This clarifies implementation of the module-specific transformations already described in v1. Hardware, learning rate, batch size, 200,000 training iterations, and training-time disclosures are unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography contains the same works. v2 expands the contrast with Gao et al. (2021) and Xu et al. (2022) by enumerating their place-cell assumptions, and Appendix A.1 adds discussion of Schaeffer et al. (2023) and complementarity with prior approaches. These are focused positioning changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the theoretical narrative is reorganized. Limitations move from Section 6 to Appendix A.2, the permutation-group discussion moves from Section 4.4 to Appendix A.7, and conformal-modulation implementation is consolidated with the multi-module appendix. The restructuring extends beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adds the learned-displacement plot and two neural-recording figure pairs as Figures 4, 5, and 11, while removing v1's square/hexagon schematic and polar isotropy plot. Retained figures are resized or repositioned, including an aspect-ratio adjustment in Figure 2(a). The existing numerical tables and path-integration graphic retain their content.

improvement.justification: The new checks on learned representations and two recorded modules strengthen empirical grounding, while the asymptotic definition improves mathematical precision. However, the promoted optimality claim exceeds the fourth-order, fixed-average-curvature argument in Section 4.4, which does not establish minimization of the full training loss at arbitrary displacements. The empirical and explanatory gains support a limited overall improvement.
